extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in comedy, free speech, and cultural/political commentary (likely conservative-leaning); comedians and cultural critics
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion-piece rubric-style critique arguing that contemporary left-wing politics has corrupted comedy — turning it from provoking laughter into enforcing political conformity and moral grandstanding. It evaluates what good comedy should be and what harms it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedian's traditional role (court jester)
rubrics_metrics.description: The old role of the comedian was as a court jester: 'shocking and amusing for its own sake' — challenging authority and saying dangerous things that make people laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author contrasts this with the modern role of the comedian as an anchorman delivering talking points. Good comedy should shock and amuse rather than simply repeat received political messages. Example language: 'The old role of the comedian as a court jester, shocking and amusing for its own sake, was replaced by the new role of the comedian as an anchorman, delivering the same talking points with more jokes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should provoke laughter, not moral applause
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy's primary aim is to make people laugh, not to summon tears or applause for the comedian's politics or personal victimhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticizes specials like Netflix’s Nanette where the comedian 'stops being funny' and is instead expected to elicit outrage or tears. 'You’re not supposed to laugh at Gadsby, but cry and be outraged at her life of oppression.' The piece treats turning comedy into a platform for moral grandstanding as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing comedy to political sermonizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy that functions mainly as a political tirade or identity-politics recitation ceases to be comedic; it becomes an ideological performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues political comedy has 'no room for going off message' and that the distinction between joking about a subject and ranting about it has eroded. Political comedy should not simply be 'angry activists who do talking points, not jokes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow offensive setup to lead to a corrective point ('offensive on your way to being inoffensive')
rubrics_metrics.description: A historically valid comic technique is to be 'offensive on your way to being inoffensive': invoke stereotypes or shock to ultimately affirm a larger, morally correct idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include All in the Family and South Park. The piece defends this technique as a way writers and comedians bypassed censorship and made moral points by portraying immorality only to ultimately uphold virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic independence from enforced ideological conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians should not be forced to have the 'right message' to be allowed to perform; comedy should not be a tribal litmus test for ideological purity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states modern leftism expects total compliance with its speech codes: 'If you were making a joke, it had better have the right message. Or else.' Failure to conform leads to sanction or cancellation (examples: Norm MacDonald, Jimmy Fallon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to the 'outrage machine' and social-media mob enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The social-media outrage machine punishes comedians who question prevailing movements or narratives, leading to cancellations and career consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm MacDonald being pulled from The Tonight Show and pressure on Netflix to cancel shows are cited. The author claims the mob 'never forgets or forgives' and that apologies often do not avert punishment: 'The outrage machine never forgets or forgives. If it fails once, it bides its time and tries again.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience expectation: audiences come to comedy for laughs, not sensitivity-catering
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences attend comedy to be entertained; catering to sensitivities and safe-space sensibilities undermines comedic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece critiques campus-style 'safe spaces and trigger warnings' and claims 'Audiences don’t go to comedy shows to have their sensitivities catered to.' This is offered as a standard for what comedy should deliver to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comics must be able to question movements and powerful trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of comedy’s social function is to question movements, popular narratives, and power structures rather than affirm them uncritically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm MacDonald’s jokes questioning #MeToo and expressing skepticism are defended as legitimate comedic inquiry. The author argues punishing such questioning is antithetical to comedy's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political comedy should not assume all humor is political
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption that every joke must carry a political message dilutes comedy and constrains comedians to ideological boxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article blames Trolls like Jon Stewart and Stephen Colbert for politicizing comedy and then notes how that led to expecting all comedy to be political: 'It assumed that all comedy was political. If you were making a joke, it had better have the right message.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative movements should not be regulated after being exploited
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a political movement uses the disruptive power of comedy, it should not then seek to restrict and control comedy after 'winning' — that is hypocrisy and kills creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's formulation: 'Leftist tyranny is born out of creative ferment and then locks it away once it wins.' The left 'exploited the destructive powers of comedy to take apart the values...' then wants 'comedy control.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Purging non-compliant comedians is a sign of cultural decline
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing comedians who make jokes with activists who deliver talking points and moralizing rants signals a loss of comedic quality and freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the treatment of Norm MacDonald, Louis C.K., and Roseanne Barr; the author argues these purges produce 'angry activists who do talking points, not jokes' and are 'as humorless as any fanatic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Apologies and appeasement often fail to placate the outrage mob
rubrics_metrics.description: Public apologies or attempts to conform after an incident may not restore a comedian’s standing because the outrage machine seeks permanent consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Norm MacDonald was 'forced to apologize' yet still faced cancellation; Jimmy Fallon's apology and retreats did not prevent continued targeting. 'No matter how much Fallon attacks Trump, he has never been forgiven for his original sin.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic/demographic differences affect comedy's safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is becoming 'safer' for certain (urban, left-leaning) audiences who expect compliance, but this makes it more dangerous for comedians overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author observes: 'Comedy is becoming safer for audiences (at least urban audiences on the left who check the headlines each morning...) and more dangerous for comedians,' implying evaluators should consider audience composition when assessing comedic risks and value.
